source.title: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations
source.authors: Rico Angell; Jannik Brinkmann; He He

record.tranche_reason: The study tests jailbreak effectiveness and transfer using multi-sample harmful-response judgments and benign-data distillation, rather than reproducing the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper tests jailbreaks, their transfer across models, and how distillation changes attack outcomes. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, or whether safety is localized in parameters. Many attack prompts are included as examples; those quoted prompts do not count as instructions addressed to a reviewing AI.
record.test_reason: The study measures how jailbreaks transfer across 20 models: similarity versus transfer AUROC, transfer after distillation, and persona versus cipher transfer reach. None of these measures what a version names. There is no harmful-data fine-tuning (V1) or token-position KL (V3). There is no separate result on prefill, suffix or decoding attacks defeating refusal (V4). It tests no parameter localization (V5), cause of shallowness (V6) or deepening method (V7). The distillation fine-tuning mixed 5,120 student harmful-instruction refusals into the 52K Alpaca data to keep safeguards. So it is not a test of benign data eroding safety (V2). It is a mitigation-style mixture, and the AIM result cannot separate distillation from the added refusal data. Refusal-direction ablation and GCG serve only as tools to build adaptive attacks. Prefilling (Qi et al. 2024) is only mentioned in background.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude jailbreak transfer emerges from shared representations plus source jailbreak strength. Distillation on teacher benign responses raises similarity and transfer, and can also pass on resistance to persona attacks such as AIM. They advocate external safeguards. The paraphrase should note that the 'benign-only' distillation corpus also contained student-generated refusals to harmful prompts.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines cross-model jailbreak transfer and representation similarity, with distillation experiments; it does not reproduce either original paper’s fine-tuning or token-depth measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported transfer varies by jailbreak type and source-strength threshold. The study also notes that evaluation depends on the judge and sampling; weaker judges overestimate transferability. Distillation is tested with three teacher–student pairs and one training configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher benign-prompt representational similarity predicts higher jailbreak transfer AUROC. The relation is tighter among models of 14B or more.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak transferability between models tracks shared representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Distillation on teacher Alpaca responses plus student refusals raises similarity. It also raises transfer of both fixed StrongREJECT jailbreaks and GCG adaptive attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing representational similarity via distillation causally increases jailbreak transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: After distillation with refusal data mixed in, Qwen2.5-7B becomes less vulnerable to AIM than before.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation toward a safer teacher can transfer resistance to persona jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: Persona jailbreaks transfer about 5–6 times more widely than cipher or direct attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-language persona jailbreaks transfer more than cipher attacks.

record.problems: The distillation experiments cover only three teacher–student pairs, one epoch, and one hyperparameter setting. Only one adaptive attack type is tested on distilled models. Several plotted results have no numeric values stated in the text. The paper notes that judge choice can materially affect estimated jailbreak effectiveness.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported result was omitted. Figure-only curves are recorded as trends where the text states their direction rather than transcribing plotted coordinates.

missing.what: Per-model success and strength for prefix_injection, refusal_suppression, style_injection and GCG transfer suffix attacks across 20 models. These are figure-only heatmaps with no numbers in the text, and could bear on V4 if read from the figure or data.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 'challenges' label is dropped. The training mixed in 5,120 harmful-prompt refusal pairs specifically to preserve safety, so the AIM decrease does not test benign fine-tuning erosion. The V4 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are dropped because the rows measure cross-model transfer or persona attacks, not opening-bypass. The Qi et al. 2023 and 2024 originals are cited only in passing.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples to measure whether refusal is removed.
Tests benign-only distillation in one teacher–student pair with AIM attacks, not a range of ordinary or carefully selected benign datasets or general harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. It tests jailbreak attacks, including suffix-based active attacks and other attack types.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety is shallow or whether data or training objectives produce shallowness.
Does not test training designed to spread safety beyond initial tokens or its robustness.

rows.subject: 20 open-weight instruction-tuned models (380 model pairs; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise representation similarity with symmetric transfer AUROC for StrongREJECT jailbreaks.
rows.measure: Relationship between pairwise model similarity and symmetric transfer AUROC
rows.value: figure only; text states that highly similar pairs never have weak transfer
rows.note: Each plotted point represents a model pair. The text reports the no-high-similarity/low-transfer pattern but gives no numeric AUROC values for the points.
rows.check: Measures the correlation between representational similarity and transfer AUROC, which is jailbreak transferability, not opening-bypass of refusal. Figure only, no numbers.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5-7B distilled on benign-only responses from Llama3.1-8B, evaluated with AIM
reader_labels.reason: The reported AIM strength falls and AIM success ends below the original student’s level, rather than rising; see R9–R10.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested jailbreak attacks, including persona attacks and GCG suffix attacks
reader_labels.reason: Jailbreaks transfer across models, transfer increases after distillation, and some tested attacks reach 100% success on particular models; see R1–R8 and R11, R13, R15–R18.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Direct or cipher-style attacks and higher source-strength thresholds
reader_labels.reason: Transfer reach is limited and lower for direct/cipher-style attacks; even persona transfer reaches only a minority at the higher threshold; see R12–R14.
